title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A mosaic of data visualizations, R code, and a GitHub repository structure, representing the complete reproducible data science workflow built over 16 weeks.
Speaker Notes: These slides guide the capstone showcase session, which includes a course retrospective, student presentations, an independent reproducibility check, and a closing reflection.


Speaker Notes: Welcome to the last class. There is no new code today. Instead, we are doing something harder — we are going to prove that the work we produced actually does what we claim it does, on a machine we have never touched.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
How To Use Today

Treat the showcase like a reproducibility audit, not a performance.
Check that the repo works from a fresh clone before you present.
Use the reflection to name one concrete improvement you would make next time.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Where We Started

Week 1: Loading one CSV without crashing R.
Week 2: Understanding what your data actually contains.
Week 3: Reading messy files into a tidy format.
Week 4: Building a plot that tells a story.


Speaker Notes: Take a moment to think back to Week 1. Most of you had never used a project-relative path. Some of you had never used R at all. The gap between where you started and where you are today is real — and it is worth naming before we move on.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
The Middle Arc

Week 5–6: Transforming and summarizing data with dplyr.
Week 7–8: Reshaping and joining datasets.
Week 9: Integrating multiple tools into one workflow.
Week 10–11: Working with strings and dates.


Speaker Notes: The middle weeks were about precision — learning that raw data almost never arrives in the shape you need it. dplyr, tidyr, and the string/date tools are what let you go from “I have data” to “I have the right data in the right format.”

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
The Advanced Arc

Week 12: Importing complex and multi-sheet data.
Week 13: Writing your own functions.
Week 14: Building reproducible reports with Quarto.
Week 15: Iteration and automation with purrr.


Speaker Notes: The back half of the semester was about scale and robustness. Functions and iteration mean you never write the same transformation twice. Quarto means your analysis and your report are the same document — there is no copy-paste gap where errors hide.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Today: The Capstone

Course retrospective — 10 minutes
Student presentations — ~10 minutes each
Independent reproducibility check — 20 minutes
Reflection and close — 20 minutes


Speaker Notes: The structure today is designed so that the reproducibility check is not just a formality — it is the proof of concept. Someone who was not in this class should be able to clone your repo and reproduce your results without asking you a single question.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Showcase Format
Each presenter has 10 minutes:

3 min: Research question and dataset overview
3 min: Walk through one key result or visualization
2 min: Walk through the repo structure (README, file paths, data)
2 min: Peer Q&A


Speaker Notes: The three-minute limit on the repo walk-through is intentional. If a colleague cannot understand your repo structure in three minutes, the README needs work. The peer Q&A should focus on one of these two questions: “What does this analysis do well?” and “What question can the data not answer?”

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Reproducibility Check Protocol
The reproducer (not the presenter) runs these steps:

git clone [repo URL] — clone to a new folder
Open the .Rproj file (not the .qmd directly)
Run renv::restore() if applicable
Render: quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd")
Verify: do figures match? any path errors?


Speaker Notes: Emphasize Step 2 — opening the .Rproj file is what sets the working directory correctly. Students who skip this step and open the .qmd directly from Finder or Windows Explorer are the ones who hit “file not found” errors even on their own machine. The reproducer should narrate what they see as they go so the presenter can take notes.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
What We Are Looking For



Check
Pass
Flag




Renders without edits
No errors
Any error


File paths
here::here() used
Absolute paths


Data present
All files tracked
Missing CSVs


Figures match
Identical to slides
Different outputs




Speaker Notes: An error during the reproducibility check is not a failure of the presenter as a person — it is a gap in the workflow. The goal is to name it precisely so it can be fixed before the Dec 14 submission. Common causes: absolute path, missing data file, package installed locally but not declared.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Final Submission Checklist

Renders clean from a fresh clone
All data files are in the repo
No absolute paths — here::here() throughout
README explains the project and how to reproduce it
Every figure has a fig-cap that describes the pattern
Interpretations match what the figures show
AI use documented if applicable
You can describe one decision you would change in a future version


Speaker Notes: Go through this checklist out loud with the class. Ask for a show of hands on each item — not to shame anyone, but to help students self-triage before the final push. The most common last-minute fix is adding or updating the README.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Reflection Prompt
“What would you do differently?”
Think about: - A skill you wish you had learned earlier - A decision in your project you would change - A question your data raised that you cannot yet answer

Speaker Notes: Give students two minutes of quiet to write before opening this to discussion. The “what would you do differently” question is more productive than “what went wrong” — it is forward-facing and normalizes iteration. There is no analysis that could not be improved with more time. The skill is knowing how you would improve it.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
What Comes Next

Dec 14: Final submission due (11:59 PM)
Push rendered .html and .qmd to GitHub Classroom
Grading rubric: Reproducibility (50), Data Management (40), Visualization (40), Communication (40), Code Quality (30)


Speaker Notes: The grading rubric weights reproducibility highest because it is the foundation of everything else. A beautiful visualization that cannot be recreated is anecdote, not analysis. Remind students that the rendered HTML must be pushed — not just the .qmd — because the grader will check the rendered output as well as the code.

title: Week 16: Capstone Showcase
text:
Thank You

You came in with a dataset and a question.
You leave with a reproducible, documented, shareable analysis.
That is not a small thing.


Speaker Notes: Close by naming something concrete the cohort improved on over the semester. Examples: “In September, half your repos had absolute paths. Today, every single one uses here().” Or: “The figure captions in your final projects are more precise than the ones in published papers I reviewed this year.” Specific praise lands harder than general praise.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A side-by-side comparison of a raw Quarto document output and a polished, formatted report with a table of contents, numbered sections, and captioned figures.
Speaker Notes: These slides guide students through progressively polishing a Quarto document from a functional draft to a reader-facing report suitable for a thesis chapter or technical memo.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Learning Objectives

Set document-level YAML options that control structure and code visibility.
Add figure and table captions with cross-references (@fig-, @tbl-).
Embed live data summaries using inline R expressions.
Create a parameterized report that can be rerun for different subgroups.
Format tables with knitr::kable() or gt().


Speaker Notes: This is Week 14 — the capstone week for reproducible workflows. Students have been writing Quarto documents all semester, but mostly for their own use. Today the audience shifts: we are writing for a reader who does not see the code. Every decision — hiding code, numbering sections, captioning figures — serves that reader.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
The Problem with Drafts

Raw output: code visible, figures unnumbered, tables print as tibbles.
A reader cannot find Figure 3 if there is no Figure 3.
Hard-coded numbers break the moment data changes.

Today’s goal: make the document do the bookkeeping so you don’t have to.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
How To Use Today

Start with a document that renders, then polish the reader experience.
Let Quarto number and reference figures and tables for you.
Use inline R for values that should stay in sync with the data.


Speaker Notes: Open a “before” document on the projector — one that renders but is clearly not ready for a reader. Ask students what they notice. Common answers: you can see all the R warnings, the figure is just floating there with no number, the table is just a tibble dump. Use this as the motivation for every YAML option we add today.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Document-Level YAML: The Foundation
---
title: "Nebraska Deer Harvest Report"
author: "Chris Chizinski"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    fig-width: 7
    fig-height: 4.5
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Speaker Notes: Walk through each option. toc: true adds the sidebar navigation — readers can jump to a section. number-sections: true auto-numbers headings. embed-resources: true is critical: without it, sharing the HTML file means sharing a folder of assets too. echo: false at the document level means no code chunks appear in the output unless a specific chunk overrides with echo: true.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
YAML Options at a Glance








Option
Where
Effect

format: html:
Adds sidebar navigation


number-sections: true
format: html:

fig-width / fig-height

Speaker Notes: Stress the two-level hierarchy: document-level execute: options set the default; individual chunk #| options override. This is how you hide data-loading code but show a key analysis chunk in a methods section.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Figure Captions and Cross-References
```{r}
#| label: fig-harvest-trend
#| fig-cap: "Total Nebraska deer harvest by year across all seasons."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of deer harvest 2018–present with increasing trend."

deer |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(total = sum(harvest_count, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Total Harvest") +
  theme_minimal()
```
In prose: "As shown in @fig-harvest-trend, harvest increased..."

Speaker Notes: The label must start with fig- for figure cross-references to work. The ?@fig-harvest-trend in prose renders as “Figure 1” — or whatever number the figure actually ends up being. The payoff: if you insert a new figure earlier in the document, all the downstream numbers update automatically. You never touch the prose. This is the core value of cross-referencing.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Why Cross-References Matter

Hard-coded: “As shown in Figure 3…” → You add a figure → now it’s Figure 4 → your prose is wrong.
Cross-reference: “As shown in ?@fig-harvest-trend…” → Quarto handles the number → always correct.

Same logic applies to tables with @tbl-.

Speaker Notes: Ask students how many times they have had to manually renumber figures in a Word document. The groan is universal. This is the exact problem cross-references solve. It is not a cosmetic feature — it is a correctness feature.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
Week 14: Polished Reporting
section: Inline R: Let the Data Write the Numbers
text:
Inline R: Let the Data Write the Numbers
In your .qmd prose:
The dataset covers `r n_distinct(deer$county)` counties and
`r n_distinct(deer$year)` harvest years, totalling
`r format(sum(deer$harvest_count, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")`
individual deer harvested.
Renders as:

The dataset covers 12 counties and 5 harvest years, totalling 48,302 individual deer harvested.


Speaker Notes: The backtick-r syntax is how Quarto evaluates R code inline inside prose. Everything between the backticks runs as R. The result is inserted as plain text. Key point: when the data is updated next year, the numbers update automatically on the next render. No search-and-replace, no copy-paste errors. Ask students: “When would hard-coding the number be safer?” Answer: when the calculation is complex enough that an error would go unnoticed — then you want to compute it once, assign it to a named object, and reference the object inline.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Parameterized Reports
params:
  county: "Lancaster"
  season: "archery"
deer_sub <- deer |>
  filter(county == params$county,
         season == params$season)
Rerun for a different county at the terminal:
quarto render report.qmd -P county:Douglas -P season:firearm

Speaker Notes: Ask: how many Nebraska counties are there? 93. If you needed a harvest report for every county, the copy-paste approach means 93 files with duplicated code, all of which drift out of sync. With params, you write one document and render it 93 times — or use a loop in a separate script to do it automatically. This is the gateway concept to literate programming at scale.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
The Report Polish Challenge

Take your capstone analysis draft (or the deer harvest starter).
Add: toc, number-sections, echo: false.
Add one figure with fig-cap and reference it with @fig- in prose.
Add one table using knitr::kable() with tbl-cap and @tbl- cross-reference.
Add two inline R expressions reporting summary values.
Add a params: block with one parameter.

Base goal: Make the draft readable and correctly referenced.
Extension goal: Parameterize the report so it can be rerun for different subgroups.

Speaker Notes: Students who do not have a capstone draft ready should use the provided deer harvest starter .qmd. The challenge is designed to be completed in one session — the pieces are all covered in today’s demo. Circulate and watch for the two most common errors: (1) labels that don’t start with fig- or tbl-, and (2) inline expressions that fail because the object isn’t defined earlier in the document.

title: Week 14: Polished Reporting
text:
Verification

Render from a fresh R session (Session > Restart R > Render).
All @fig- and @tbl- references resolve — no ?fig- in the output.
Inline R values match what you see in the console.
The TOC has at least three entries.
params block is tested with at least two different values.
Can you explain why hard-coded figure numbers are a maintenance problem?


Speaker Notes: The restart-and-render test is the gold standard for reproducibility. If the document only renders when your environment is already populated, it is not reproducible — it just looks like it is. Emphasize this before students submit their assignments: render from a clean session, not from the comfort of an open session where everything is already loaded.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A branching diagram showing three separate CSV files converging into a single unified data frame, representing the programmatic reading of multiple files.
Speaker Notes: These slides teach students to replace repetitive file-reading code with a functional iteration pattern using purrr::map() and fs::dir_ls().

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
The Copy-Paste Trap

Year 1: you copy one read_csv() call.
Year 2: you paste and change “2021” to “2022”.
Year 3: you do it again.
Year 4: a colleague adds a file. You forget to update the script.

This is the copy-paste anti-pattern. It scales badly and breaks silently.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
How To Use Today

Replace repetition with a pattern that adapts to new files.
Keep track of where each row came from.
Inspect mismatched columns before you drop or rename anything.


Speaker Notes: Ask: “How many of you have done this?” Almost everyone will raise a hand. The key insight is that copying code isn’t just an aesthetic problem — it’s a correctness problem. When the folder gains a new file, the manually-maintained script is instantly out of date. The goal today is to make the script adapt automatically.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Learning Objectives

Use fs::dir_ls() to list files programmatically.
Use purrr::map() + list_rbind() to read multiple files without copy-paste.
Track the source file name with the .id argument.
Detect and handle column mismatches across files.
Read specific sheets from Excel workbooks with readxl::read_excel().


Speaker Notes: These five skills are what separate a script that runs once from a pipeline that keeps running as data accumulates. By the end of class, students should be able to drop a new CSV in the data folder and re-run the script with zero code changes.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
The Anti-Pattern vs The Pattern


Anti-pattern (copy-paste)
d21 <- read_csv("counts_2021.csv")
d22 <- read_csv("counts_2022.csv")
d23 <- read_csv("counts_2023.csv")
all <- bind_rows(d21, d22, d23)
Adding year 4 = editing 2 lines.

Pattern (iterate)
files <- dir_ls("data", glob = "*.csv")
all   <- files |>
  map(read_csv) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "source_file")
Adding year 4 = zero code changes.


Speaker Notes: Put both blocks on screen at the same time so students can compare them side by side. The left is familiar; the right is unfamiliar but shorter. Emphasize that the right side is not shorter because it is clever — it is shorter because it describes the pattern rather than the instances. Ask: “What has to be true about the files for the right-hand pattern to work?” Answer: they must live in the same folder and have the same naming convention.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
fs::dir_ls() — File Discovery
library(fs)

csv_files <- dir_ls(here("data"), glob = "*.csv")
csv_files
#> data/annual_counts_2021.csv
#> data/annual_counts_2022.csv
#> data/annual_counts_2023.csv

glob = "*.csv" filters by file pattern (shell-style wildcard).
Returns an fs_path vector — works like a character vector, prints cleanly.
Change the glob and the rest of the pipeline updates automatically.


Speaker Notes: Run this live. Students often think of file-listing as something you do in Finder or the terminal. Show them that R can see the filesystem too. Emphasize the glob argument — this is how they would limit to a specific pattern like “raptor_*.csv” if the folder contained mixed file types.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
section: purrr::map() — Applying a Function to Every Element
text:
purrr::map() — Applying a Function to Every Element
library(purrr)

# map() returns a *list* — one data frame per file
list_of_dfs <- map(csv_files, read_csv)
length(list_of_dfs)   # 3
class(list_of_dfs)    # "list"

# list_rbind() collapses the list into one data frame
all_counts <- list_rbind(list_of_dfs, names_to = "source_file")
nrow(all_counts)      # 90

Speaker Notes: Slow down here. Students who have not seen functional programming before will find this abstract. The key mental model: map() is a loop that saves the output. Ask: “What would you have to do with a for-loop to get the same result?” Then show them that map() + list_rbind() does the same thing in two lines. The names_to argument is critical — if you skip it, you lose the information about which file each row came from.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Tracking the Source File with .id
all_counts <- csv_files |>
  map(read_csv) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "source_file")

# Extract the year from the file path
all_counts <- all_counts |>
  mutate(year = str_extract(source_file, "\\d{4}") |> as.integer())

names_to = "source_file" stores the file path in a new column.
str_extract() pulls the 4-digit year from the path string.
Without this step: all your rows look identical and the year is lost.


Speaker Notes: This is a step students frequently skip because they think they can infer the year from the data itself. But survey_date only tells you when the survey happened — not which file it came from. What if you had a bug that read the wrong file? The source_file column is your audit trail. Make the habit explicit.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Column Mismatches Happen
The 2023 file has a notes column. The 2021 and 2022 files do not.
all_counts |> count(source_file, is.na(notes))
#> annual_counts_2021.csv  TRUE   30
#> annual_counts_2022.csv  TRUE   30
#> annual_counts_2023.csv  FALSE  30
list_rbind() fills missing columns with NA — this is correct behavior.
Your job: understand the NAs before you drop or ignore them.

Speaker Notes: Students often panic when they see a column of NAs. Teach them the diagnostic reflex: count(source_file, is.na(column)) before making any decisions. In this case the NAs are completely explainable — 2021 and 2022 didn’t record observer notes. The next question is whether notes matters for the analysis. Since we are summarizing counts, we can safely drop it. But we document why.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Reading Excel: readxl::read_excel()
library(readxl)

# ALWAYS inspect sheet names first
excel_sheets(here("data", "monitoring_workbook.xlsx"))
#> [1] "Cover"            "Raptor Survey"
#> [3] "Waterfowl Survey" "Metadata"

# Read a specific sheet by name
raptors <- read_excel(
  here("data", "monitoring_workbook.xlsx"),
  sheet = "Raptor Survey"
)
Omitting sheet = reads the first sheet only — which is often a cover page.

Speaker Notes: Ask: “Has anyone ever opened an Excel file in R and wondered why there was no data?” This is almost always the cause. The default reads sheet 1, which in monitoring workbooks is often a title or cover sheet with no data. Show excel_sheets() as the first thing to run whenever you receive a new workbook. It is cheap — it just reads the sheet names, not the data.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
section: Reading All Excel Sheets at Once
text:
Reading All Excel Sheets at Once
path <- here("data", "monitoring_workbook.xlsx")

all_sheets <- excel_sheets(path) |>
  map(\(s) read_excel(path, sheet = s)) |>
  set_names(excel_sheets(path))

# Access by name
all_sheets[["Raptor Survey"]]
Same map() pattern — now applied to sheet names instead of file paths.

Speaker Notes: Point out the parallel structure: in one case we mapped over file paths; here we map over sheet names. The function we apply is different but the pattern is identical. This is why learning map() once pays dividends — it generalizes to any situation where you want to apply the same function to a list of inputs.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Three-Year Monitoring Audit
You have three years of annual wildlife count CSV files.
Question: How has total species count changed across sites from 2021 to 2023?
Must use: dir_ls(), map(), list_rbind(), year extraction, and a trend plot.
Base goal: Read all three files and produce one combined table.
Extension goal: Add the source file or year to your plot and explain the trend.

Speaker Notes: Remind students that the 2023 file has the extra notes column — this is intentional. They need to detect it, understand it, and handle it before summarizing. The plot should show year on the x-axis, total count on the y-axis, and lines colored by site. Students who finish early can add n_species as a secondary facet or extend with error bars.

title: Week 12: Scaling Up
text:
Verification

Does your combined data frame have exactly 90 rows and rows from all 3 years?
Did you check for NAs in the notes column and document where they came from?
Does your trend plot have axis labels, a title, and theme_minimal()?
If a annual_counts_2024.csv appeared in the folder tomorrow, how many lines of your script would you need to change?
Can you explain why map() is better than copy-paste here?


Speaker Notes: The last question is the key verification. The answer should be zero — if they have to change even one line, their pipeline is not fully generalized. Go around the room and have each student answer it aloud. This reinforces the central lesson: we write code that adapts, not code that we maintain by hand.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A screenshot of a messy CSV file with inconsistent capitalization and extra spaces in a state code column, beside a clean version of the same table after string standardization.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce systematic text cleaning using stringr functions, janitor column name normalization, and factor reordering with forcats.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Where We Are

Week 09: You tackled your first fully messy dataset — end to end.
This week: We name the specific tools for the most common mess.
The trio: stringr (text), janitor (column names), forcats (categories).

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
How To Use Today

Clean column names first so the rest of the script stays readable.
Standardize text before grouping or plotting.
Reorder factors when the default alphabetical order would mislead.


Speaker Notes: Last week you encountered messy data for the first time in a systematic way. You probably noticed that a lot of the mess was text — inconsistent capitalization, extra spaces, abbreviated versus spelled-out values. This week we put names on those problems and give you a repeatable toolkit. These three packages together handle the vast majority of text and categorical cleanup you will encounter in ecological and agricultural data.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Learning Objectives

Use janitor::clean_names() to normalize column names on import.
Apply str_trim(), str_to_lower(), and str_to_upper() to standardize text fields.
Use str_detect() for partial-match filtering and str_replace() for targeted recoding.
Control factor level order in plots using fct_reorder() and fct_relevel().


Speaker Notes: Four objectives, roughly one per 30-minute block of live coding today. Objective 4 — factor reordering — is the one that immediately improves the quality of every visualization they make, so it tends to get the most audible reaction in class. Let students work through the alphabetical-order plot first, then show the reordered version.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
section: The Problem: Text Columns Are Liars
text:
The Problem: Text Columns Are Liars
count(crop_raw, state)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
#   state        n
#   <chr>    <int>
# 1 NE          20
# 2 ne          20
# 3 Nebraska    20
# 4 NEBRASKA    20
One state. Four representations. Every group_by() will treat them as four groups.

Speaker Notes: Pull this up in the console and run it live. Ask the class: if we group_by(state) right now and calculate a mean, how many rows will we get? They will say four. Then ask: how many should we get? One. That’s the whole problem — and it’s invisible unless you look. This slide exists to make them paranoid. Good paranoid.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Tool 1: janitor::clean_names()
library(janitor)

crop_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "crop_survey_messy.csv")) |>
  clean_names()

Converts Reported Yield Bu/Ac → reported_yield_bu_ac
No more backtick-quoting column names in your pipeline.
Always do this on import.


Speaker Notes: clean_names() is a one-line, no-brainer addition to every import. It handles spaces, special characters, and mixed case in column headers. The rule of thumb I give students: if the column name would need backticks in R, clean_names() would have fixed it. Make it a habit — add it to your import template.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Tool 2: str_trim() and str_to_lower()
library(stringr)

crop_clean <- crop_raw |>
  mutate(
    state = str_trim(state) |> str_to_lower(),
    crop_type = str_trim(crop_type) |> str_to_lower()
  )
Order matters: trim whitespace FIRST, then change case.

Speaker Notes: Ask the class: why does order matter here? If you lower-case first, you still have “corn” with a trailing space. When you group by it, “corn” and “corn” are different values. Trim first eliminates the space, then lower-case standardizes capitalization. The trailing space is especially insidious because it is invisible in the output — you have to count characters or look at the raw CSV to find it. That’s the kind of bug that costs an afternoon.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Tool 3: str_replace()
crop_clean <- crop_clean |>
  mutate(
    state = str_replace(state, "nebraska", "ne"),
    crop_type = str_replace(crop_type, "^soy$", "soybean"),
    crop_type = str_replace(crop_type, "soybeans", "soybean")
  )

^soy$ anchors the pattern — matches the whole word only.
Without anchors, str_replace("soybean", "soy", "X") → "Xbean".


Speaker Notes: The regex anchors ^ and $ are the most important thing to explain here. Write “soy” on the board or slide, then show what happens if you replace “soy” inside “soybean” without anchors. The result is “Xbean”, which is wrong. The anchors say “only match if soy is the entire string.” This is a common mistake. You can also show str_replace_all() versus str_replace() — the former replaces every match in the string, the latter only the first. For cleaning categorical labels we almost always want str_replace().

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Tool 4: str_detect() for Filtering
# Filter rows where notes mention irrigation
crop_clean |>
  filter(str_detect(notes, "irrigat")) |>
  select(county, crop_type, notes)

Returns TRUE/FALSE — works inside filter() naturally.
Pattern is a regular expression — "irrigat" matches “irrigated”, “irrigation”, etc.


Speaker Notes: str_detect() is the partial-match filter. Contrast it with the equality filter: filter(state == “ne”) only matches exact strings. str_detect() matches substrings or patterns. The notes column in today’s dataset is a good example — no two notes are identical, but you can still find rows mentioning irrigation, drought, or flood damage. This is also useful for sanity checking: str_detect(crop_type, ” “) will catch any values that still have spaces in them after cleaning.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Tool 5: fct_reorder() and fct_relevel()
library(forcats)

# Logical order: small -> medium -> large
crop_summary <- crop_summary |>
  mutate(
    farm_size_category = fct_relevel(farm_size_category,
                                     "small", "medium", "large")
  )

fct_relevel(): set an explicit, meaningful order.
fct_reorder(): sort by a numeric variable (e.g., mean yield, descending).


Speaker Notes: ggplot defaults to alphabetical factor order. For farm size, alphabetical gives you “large, medium, small” — the reverse of what anyone expects. fct_relevel() lets you specify exactly what order the levels appear. fct_reorder() is used when the order should be driven by a numeric value, like ranking crop types from highest to lowest yield. Show both: fct_relevel for ordinal categories with a natural order, fct_reorder for nominal categories ranked by a statistic.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
Before and After: Factor Order
# Before: alphabetical (confusing)
ggplot(crop_summary, aes(x = farm_size_category, y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_col()

# After: logical order (clear)
crop_summary |>
  mutate(farm_size_category = fct_relevel(farm_size_category,
                                          "small", "medium", "large")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = farm_size_category, y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_col()

Speaker Notes: Run both plots side by side if you can. The alphabetical version reads “large, medium, small” which forces the audience to mentally reorder while reading. The reordered version reads left to right in the natural direction. This is a small change with a large communication payoff. Make the point that factor reordering is not cosmetic — it changes what conclusions readers draw from the chart.

title: Week 10: String Cleaning and Categorical Control
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Crop Yield Audit

Clean the crop_survey_messy.csv dataset end to end.
Base goal: Which crop type has the highest average yield in Nebraska?
Extension goal: Does farm size matter once the categories are ordered clearly?
Required: clean text columns, filter to NE, summarize, plot with reordered factors.


Speaker Notes: Students should be able to complete this independently now — they have all four tools. The challenge is intentionally structured so that cleaning must happen before the analysis makes sense. If they skip cleaning and go straight to group_by(), they will get four state groups instead of one and their results will be wrong. That is the lesson. Walk the room during the 45 minutes and look for students who are still getting four crop_type values after their clean step — that means they missed either str_trim() or the anchored str_replace().

Verification

Does count(crop_clean, crop_type) show exactly two values?
Is your x-axis ordered small → medium → large (not alphabetical)?

Speaker Notes: Go through each verification check with the class before they commit. The count checks are pass/fail — if they have more than one state value, their pipeline has a bug. The ordering check is about communication quality. The articulation question is the metacognitive exit ticket: if they can explain the order-of-operations logic, they will apply it correctly to future datasets without needing to be reminded.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A two-table diagram showing an observations table on the left and a site metadata table on the right, connected by a shared site_id key column, representing the concept of relational data joining.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce the three core join operations in dplyr — left_join, inner_join, and anti_join — using bird observation data joined to site metadata.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
How To Use Today

Identify the key column before you join anything.
Check row counts immediately after each join.
Use anti_join() when the output looks suspicious or incomplete.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Why Joins Exist

Ecological data rarely lives in one table.
Observations tell you what was seen and where.
Site metadata tells you what that place is like.
Joins link tables by a shared key column.


Speaker Notes: Think about how you would collect field data. You record species observations in one notebook. Site characteristics — habitat type, area, land use — are in a separate site registry. Keeping them separate is the right design: it avoids repeating site information on every observation row. But to answer questions like ‘which habitat type has the most species?’, you need to link those two tables together. That is exactly what a join does.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Learning Objectives

Explain what a key column is and why it must match exactly.
Use left_join() to add site context to observation records.
Use inner_join() and explain when rows are dropped.
Use anti_join() to audit unmatched records.
Verify row counts before and after every join.


Speaker Notes: By the end of today you will have a toolkit for combining any two related tables in R. More importantly, you will have the habit of checking row counts and auditing unmatched records — skills that catch data problems before they silently corrupt your analysis.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
The Key Column
# Both tables must have a column with matching values
obs   |> distinct(site_id)   # e.g., SITE001, SITE002, ...
sites |> distinct(site_id)   # e.g., SITE001, SITE002, ...

The key must be the same type in both tables (character = character).
Values must match exactly — "SITE001" ≠ "site001".
Check for duplicates in the right-hand table before joining.


Speaker Notes: Before you ever run a join, ask yourself: what is the key? In our dataset it is site_id. Now ask: does site_id appear in both tables, and do the values match exactly? A trailing space or a case difference will silently cause a row to go unmatched. This is one of the most common join bugs in practice.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
left_join: The Safe Join
Visual concept (describe aloud):

Imagine two tables side by side. The left table — your observations — is the anchor. Every row in the left table is kept. Matching rows from the right table slide in alongside. Where no match exists, the right-side columns fill with NA.

obs_with_sites <- obs |>
  left_join(sites, by = "site_id")

nrow(obs)            # e.g., 80
nrow(obs_with_sites) # still 80 — left table is preserved

Speaker Notes: The left join is your default join for ecological analysis. It says: ‘I want to keep all of my observation records, and I will add whatever site information I can find. If a site has no metadata, I get NA — and that NA is a signal to investigate, not a reason to lose the record.’ The key insight is that the row count of the result equals the row count of the left table, assuming no duplicate keys in the right table.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
inner_join: Only Matched Rows
obs_inner <- obs |>
  inner_join(sites, by = "site_id")

nrow(obs_inner)  # fewer rows — unmatched obs are dropped

Rows from obs with no matching site_id in sites are silently dropped.
Use when you need complete cases for a model or calculation.
Always compare nrow() before and after.


Speaker Notes: The inner join is stricter. It only keeps rows where the key exists in both tables. This can be the right choice — if you are fitting a model that requires habitat type, you cannot include sites with missing metadata. But the danger is that rows disappear silently. You must check the row count. If you expected 80 rows and got 76, ask: which 4 observations were dropped, and why?

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
anti_join: The Data Audit Tool
unmatched <- obs |>
  anti_join(sites, by = "site_id")

# Shows obs rows with no matching site in the registry
unmatched |> select(obs_id, site_id, species, date)

Returns rows from the left table that have no match in the right table.
This is your primary tool for finding data quality problems.
Ask: were these sites omitted from the registry by mistake?


Speaker Notes: The anti_join is the most underused of the three joins, and arguably the most important for data quality. Before you do any analysis, run an anti_join to find out which records have no metadata. In our dataset, SITE016 and SITE017 appear in observations but not in the site registry. Is that a data entry error? A site that was surveyed but never formally registered? You need to know before you proceed.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Row Count Verification
cat("Original observations:          ", nrow(obs), "\n")
cat("After left_join (with sites):   ", nrow(obs_with_sites), "\n")
cat("After inner_join (only matched):", nrow(obs_inner), "\n")
cat("Unmatched observations:         ", nrow(unmatched), "\n")

left_join row count = original obs count (assuming no duplicate keys in right table).
inner_join row count <= left_join count.
unmatched count = left_join count - inner_join count.


Speaker Notes: Make this a reflex: every time you join two tables, print the row counts of the input and output. If left_join produces MORE rows than your left table, you have duplicate keys in the right table — one input row matched multiple right-side rows and got duplicated. If inner_join produces fewer rows, rows were silently dropped. These are the two most common join surprises.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Load both tables and inspect dimensions.
Compare site_id values across tables.
left_join(), inner_join(), anti_join() in sequence.
Verify row counts at each step.


Speaker Notes: We will work through all three joins on the bird observation dataset. For each join, we will check the row count immediately after. I will also show you how to use filter(is.na(habitat_type)) after a left_join to locate the unmatched rows — which gives you the same information as anti_join but from the joined table perspective.

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: Habitat Richness and the Missing Registry

Base goal: Join bird observations to site metadata and audit unmatched sites using anti_join().
Extension goal: Summarize species richness by habitat type using group_by() + summarize() and visualize the distribution.


Speaker Notes: The challenge today has two parts that must be done in order. First, audit the data — find and document the sites that have observations but no registry entry. Second, join and analyze. You will calculate species richness (number of unique species) per site, then average that by habitat type. The goal is to answer the question: which habitat types support the most diverse bird communities?

title: Week 08: Joining Tables
text:
Verification

Does your left_join result have the same row count as the original obs?
Did anti_join reveal any unmatched site_id values?
Does your richness summary group correctly by habitat_type?
Does your plot have a title, axis labels, and a color scale?
Can you explain why left_join() is the safest default for this task?


Speaker Notes: Before you commit, run through this checklist out loud. The row count check is non-negotiable — if you cannot confirm the join preserved or intentionally reduced your rows, you do not know what you joined. The audit question is the analytical equivalent: if you skipped the anti_join, you do not know whether your richness estimates are based on complete data.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A field notebook showing a tally of bird species counts next to a laptop screen with an R console, representing the shift from raw observations to grouped summaries.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce group_by() and summarize() as the core dplyr tools for collapsing raw data into group-level answers.


Speaker Notes: Welcome to Week 06. Today we move from row-level transformations — which we did with filter, mutate, and arrange — to group-level summaries. This is one of the most powerful shifts in data analysis: going from “what do individual observations say?” to “what does each group tell us?”

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
How To Use Today

Treat each summary as a question about a group, not a row.
Predict the row count before you run summarize().
Check whether NA means missing information or a true zero.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Learning Objectives

Use group_by() to define analysis groups.
Use summarize() to collapse groups into summary statistics.
Apply n(), n_distinct(), sum(), and mean() inside summarize().
Handle missing values (NA) deliberately before summarizing.
Combine arrange(desc()) to rank grouped results.


Speaker Notes: By the end of today you should be able to take a raw dataset of thousands of rows and produce a clean ranked summary table in a single pipe chain. These five functions — group_by, summarize, n, n_distinct, and arrange — will appear in almost every data analysis project you do.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
section: Where We Are in the Pipeline
text:
Where We Are in the Pipeline
read_csv() → glimpse() → filter() → mutate() → group_by() → summarize()

Last week: filter(), select(), arrange(), mutate() — row-level operations.
This week: group_by() + summarize() — group-level operations.
Key shift: The output has fewer rows than the input.


Speaker Notes: This is the most important conceptual shift of today. Every function we’ve learned so far — filter, mutate, arrange — returns the same number of rows (or fewer via filter). Summarize intentionally collapses rows. One row per group, no matter how many observations were in that group. If this feels surprising, that’s exactly the right reaction — pause and think about it.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
section: The Mental Model: Split → Apply → Combine
text:
The Mental Model: Split → Apply → Combine

Split: group_by(species_code) divides the data into one “chunk” per species.
Apply: summarize() runs a calculation on each chunk independently.
Combine: The results are reassembled into one tidy output table.


Speaker Notes: “Split, apply, combine” is a phrase from statistics that predates R. The idea is ancient: separate your data by group, do the math on each group, then stack the results back together. group_by does the split, summarize does the apply and combine. This mental model will help you debug when results look wrong.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Multiple Summaries in One Call
birds |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(
    total_obs  = sum(how_many, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_records  = n(),
    n_sites    = n_distinct(site_id),
    mean_count = mean(how_many, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

n() counts rows in the group.
n_distinct(site_id) counts unique values of site_id in the group.


Speaker Notes: You can put as many summary expressions as you want inside a single summarize() call — each becomes one new column. Emphasize the difference between n() and n_distinct(): n() asks “how many rows?” while n_distinct() asks “how many unique values?” If site NE001 appears five times in January, n() counts 5 but n_distinct(site_id) still counts 1.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
Week 06: Grouped Summaries
section: Handling NAs: A Decision, Not a Default

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Grouping by Multiple Columns
birds |>
  group_by(state, month) |>
  summarize(
    total_obs = sum(how_many, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_sites   = n_distinct(site_id),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

Result has one row per unique combination of state and month.
.groups = "drop" removes the grouping structure after summarizing.


Speaker Notes: You can group by any number of columns. The result always has one row per unique combination of the grouping variables. Mention .groups = “drop” — without it, dplyr retains a residual grouping on all but the last variable, which can produce unexpected behavior in downstream pipes. Using drop is the safer default in most workflows.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Load feeder_watch_raw.csv and inspect with glimpse().
Run a global summarize() — predict the row count first.
Add group_by(state) and observe the change.
Build a multi-column summarize() with n(), n_distinct(), and mean().


Speaker Notes: Open week_06_instructor.R. Walk through sections 3a through 3d at a teaching pace — pause after each code chunk and ask students to predict the output before running it. The goal is to build intuition for what group_by does to the data, not to move through the code quickly.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Live Coding: Section 2

Demonstrate multi-column group_by().
Add .groups = "drop".
Rank species by total observations with arrange(desc()).
Show the NA comparison side by side.


Speaker Notes: This section reinforces the concepts with practical ranking. The NA comparison (sum with vs without na.rm) is the single most important live demo of the day — do not skip it. Ask students to explain, in plain English, why one column is NA and the other is not.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
The Wildlife Survey Audit

Dataset: feeder_watch_raw.csv
Base goal: Identify the Top 5 species observed in Nebraska during January.
Extension goal: Compare the top species by total observations and number of sites.

Steps: 1. filter() to Nebraska, January. 2. Remove NA and zero-count rows. 3. group_by() species code. 4. summarize() — create total_obs and n_sites. 5. arrange(desc()) and keep top 5.
Constraint: Use |> at least once. summarize() must produce at least 2 columns.

Speaker Notes: Release the follow-along script. Students have 45 minutes. Circulate and watch for two common errors: forgetting group_by before summarize (results in one row), and not using na.rm = TRUE (results in NA in total_obs). The verification question is on the next slide — remind students to check it before they commit.

title: Week 06: Grouped Summaries
text:
Verification

Does your final table have exactly 5 rows?
Is total_obs a number (not NA) for every row?
Did you write a comment explaining your NA decision?
Can you explain in one sentence why group_by() changed the output shape?
Compare your top species with your neighbor — do they match?


Speaker Notes: Walk around and look at screens before class ends. The most common failure mode is a table with more than 5 rows (forgot slice_head) or NA in total_obs (forgot na.rm or forgot to filter NAs first). If two neighbors get different answers, that’s a great signal to debug together — ask them to read each other’s filter conditions out loud.

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A vibrant collage of various data visualizations, including scatterplots, bar charts, and heatmaps, representing the diversity of the Grammar of Graphics.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce the core concepts of ggplot2, focusing on mapping variables to aesthetics and faceting.

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations
Week 04: Viz Foundations
text:
How To Use Today

Decide what the plot needs to say before choosing the geom.
Use color only when it helps the reader.
Prefer clear labels and a clean theme over decoration.


Speaker Notes: The question for today is not “What looks pretty?” It is “What helps the reader understand the data fastest?”

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations
text:
Mapping vs Setting

Mapping: Linking data to a visual trait (inside aes()).
Setting: Assigning a fixed visual trait (outside aes()).
This is the #1 source of ggplot confusion!


Speaker Notes: If you remember only one thing from today, let it be the difference between ‘mapping’ and ‘setting’. Mapping is when you want the color to change based on the data (like species). Setting is when you just want all the points to be blue. Mixing these up is the most common error in ggplot2.

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations
text:
Learning Objectives

Map variables to aesthetics.
Choose geoms for different data types.
Use facets to split plots by category.
Add professional labels and themes.


Speaker Notes: Today we move from simple plots to ‘publication-ready’ visualizations. We’ll learn how to choose the right ‘geom’ for your data and how to use ‘facets’ to tell a story across different categories.

Layers of a ggplot.
Histograms, Boxplots, and Scatterplots.
Faceting and Themes.


Speaker Notes: We’ll build our plots layer-by-layer. Think of it like an onion—we start with the data, then add the mapping, then the geom, then the labels, and finally the theme.

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations

The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Visualization Architect

Build a multi-layer plot of prairie restoration.
Use facets to compare soil types.
Apply a clean theme and informative labels.
Base goal: Make the plot communicate the trend clearly.
Extension goal: Add a facet-based version and compare it to the colored version.


Speaker Notes: You are now the ‘Architect’. You have a dataset of prairie restoration plots. Your goal is to build a visualization that clearly shows how species richness changes over time across different soil types.

title: Week 04: Viz Foundations

Verification

Does the plot clearly show the trend?
Are the axis labels readable and informative?
Did you use a professional theme and a color-blind-safe palette?


Speaker Notes: If the plot needs a long explanation to make sense, the design needs work. The final check is whether a first-time reader can understand it quickly.


Speaker Notes: Before you commit, look at your plot with fresh eyes. Are the axis labels large enough? Does the title actually describe what’s happening? Did you remember to use a theme like ‘theme_minimal’ to remove the default gray background?

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A close-up image of a computer screen displaying multiple R error messages in red text, symbolizing the debugging process.
Speaker Notes: These slides explain the fundamental nature of R objects and how to diagnose errors.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
How To Use Today

Read the error message before touching the code.
Use the Environment pane as a diagnostic tool.
Fix the cause, not just the symptom.


Speaker Notes: This week is about developing a debugging habit. The slides should help students remember the flow: inspect, diagnose, fix, verify.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
R is for Objects

Everything that exists in R is an object.
Everything that happens is a function.
Objects have types (numeric, character, logical).


Speaker Notes: In R, everything you create—a single number, a list of names, or a giant dataset—is an ‘object’. We interact with these objects using ‘functions’. Today we learn how to see inside these objects and understand their ‘type’.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Learning Objectives

Create and name R objects.
Identify common data types.
Inspect data frames in the Environment.
Interpret and fix common R errors.


Speaker Notes: Our goal is to move from being ‘scared’ of error messages to ‘reading’ them. By the end of today, you should be able to identify why a function fails based on the data type you give it.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Creating vectors and data frames.
Breaking R on purpose.
Interpreting error messages.


Speaker Notes: We’ll start by building vectors. Then, I’m going to ask you to try and ‘break’ your code. Intentionally causing errors is one of the best ways to learn how R thinks.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging
text:

Extension goal: Explain each fix in plain language.


Speaker Notes: In this challenge, you are playing the role of a ‘Code Doctor’. I’ve provided a script that is sick—it won’t run. Your job is to diagnose the 3 main bugs and get it back to healthy, runnable status.

title: Week 02: Objects & Debugging

Does the script run without errors from top to bottom?

Did you push a clear commit message that names what changed?


Speaker Notes: If they can explain the error in one sentence and show the fix in the script, they have met the goal for the day.

A classic dataset for learning visualization.

Did you commit and push the rendered result?

Speaker Notes: Before you leave, you must verify your work. Render the document. If it doesn’t render, we need to fix it before you go. Finally, push to GitHub. If it’s not on GitHub, it doesn’t exist for grading!

Speaker Notes: These slides cover the critical concepts of project-relative paths and data import strategies.

title: Week 03: Importing Data
Week 03: Importing Data
text:
How To Use Today

Find the project root first.
Use here() before you type a path by hand.
Verify that the raw data is still unchanged after import.


Speaker Notes: The goal today is portability. Students should leave with a workflow that works on another machine, not just the one they are using right now.

title: Week 03: Importing Data
text:
The Path to Reproducibility

Avoid absolute paths like C:/Users/Chris/Downloads.
Use the here package to find files relative to your project.
Keep your raw data “read-only”.


Speaker Notes: One of the most common reasons code fails when shared is that it uses ‘absolute paths’. If your script starts with ‘C:/Users/YourName’, it will NEVER work on my machine. We’re going to use a package called ‘here’ that builds paths relative to your project file, making your code portable and reproducible.

title: Week 03: Importing Data
text:
Learning Objectives

Explain the value of relative paths.
Use here::here() to find files.
Import CSVs with read_csv().
Skip metadata rows during import.


Speaker Notes: By the end of today, you’ll be able to move your project folder to any computer, or even share it on GitHub, and have the data load perfectly every time. We’ll also learn how to handle those annoying extra rows at the top of many CSV files.

title: Week 03: Importing Data
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Setting up the data/ folder.
Importing weather data.
Handling messy headers.
Checking the imported types and row count.


Speaker Notes: First, we’re going to create a standard ‘data’ folder. Then we’ll practice importing a weather dataset. We’ll look at the console output to see how R ‘guesses’ what kind of data is in each column.

title: Week 03: Importing Data

The Challenge [45 mins]

Import stream_gauge_messy.csv with 5 rows of metadata.
Rename the discharge column so it is easier to read.
Identify missing values or suspicious values in the imported data.

Does the script run on your neighbor’s machine?
Are you using here() and not setwd()?
