Speaker Notes: The import is not finished until you know where the file lives, how many rows came in, and whether the headers are correct.


Speaker Notes: The ultimate test of reproducibility: can your neighbor run your script? If you used ‘here()’, the answer should be yes. Check your ‘data’ folder—did you include the raw CSV?

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A map of Nebraska counties overlaid with colored circles representing deer harvest counts by region and year, illustrating spatial and temporal variation in wildlife data.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce the four core dplyr verbs — filter, select, arrange, and mutate — using Nebraska deer harvest records as the working dataset.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
How To Use Today

Treat each verb as a tool with one job.
Ask which rows or columns should change before typing.
Check the row count after every major filter.


Speaker Notes: This week is about changing the shape of the data without losing track of what each step does. Keep the verbs separate in your mind: filter for rows, select for columns, arrange for order, mutate for new variables.


Speaker Notes: Welcome to Week 05. This week we shift from visualization to transformation. Before you can build a meaningful plot, you usually have to reshape your data. The four verbs we learn today — filter, select, arrange, and mutate — will handle the vast majority of data wrangling tasks you encounter in graduate research.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
Learning Objectives

Use filter() to subset rows by one or more conditions.
Use select() to keep or rename columns.
Use arrange() to sort rows by one or more variables.
Use mutate() to create new columns from existing ones, including case_when().


Speaker Notes: These four verbs follow a consistent pattern: the first argument is always the data frame, and the output is always a new data frame. This makes them pipe-friendly. Each verb does exactly one thing — that predictability is what makes dplyr so powerful for teaching.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
The Dataset: Nebraska Deer Harvest

Source: Simulated from Nebraska Game and Parks Commission harvest structure.
Unit of observation: One row = one county × year × season × sex × age class combination.
Key variables: county, year, season, sex, age_class, harvest_count, hunter_days.
Teaching features: Includes NA values in harvest_count and hunter_days — real decisions required.


Speaker Notes: This dataset mirrors the structure of real state wildlife harvest reports. Each row is not an individual deer — it is an aggregate record for a county-season-sex-age combination. That distinction matters when students start summarizing. Point out the NA values early: they are deliberate and will force students to think about missing data decisions before they can calculate rates.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
The Four dplyr Verbs



Verb
Operation
Think of it as…




filter()
Rows
Keep only certain rows


select()
Columns
Keep only certain columns


arrange()
Order
Sort the table


mutate()
New columns
Add a calculated variable




Speaker Notes: Show this table and ask students: ‘If I want only bucks from Lancaster County, which verb do I use?’ If I want only the county and harvest columns, which verb? If I want to rank by harvest count, which verb? If I want to calculate harvest per hunter day, which verb? These four questions map cleanly to the four verbs.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Load ne_deer_harvest.csv with here().
filter(): single condition, multiple conditions, !is.na().
select() and rename columns.
arrange() with desc().
mutate() for arithmetic and case_when().


Speaker Notes: During live coding, make the == mistake on purpose when writing filter(season = “rifle”) and let R throw the error. This is the most common mistake and seeing it in context is more memorable than being warned about it. After fixing it, say: ‘In R, = means assignment; == means comparison.’

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Harvest Analyst

Question: Which NE county had the largest increase in doe harvest from 2020 to 2022?
Required verbs: filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange()
Hint: You will also need pivot_wider() to put each year in its own column before you can subtract.
Base goal: A county comparison table with the numeric change.
Extension goal: Add a percent change column and explain whether the biggest absolute change is also the biggest relative change.


Speaker Notes: Remind students of the constraints: they must use the native pipe |> at least once, and they must use mutate() to compute the difference — not do it by hand. The pivot_wider step is a preview of next week. Give a 2-minute explanation of pivot_wider before releasing them. The goal is not to memorize the syntax but to understand why reshaping is necessary to do column arithmetic.

title: Week 05: Rows, Columns, and New Variables
text:
Verification

Does filter() return the number of rows you expected? Check with nrow().
Did you account for missing values before calculating the comparison?
Does your final challenge table include the numeric change and the year labels?
Can you explain the difference between filter() (rows) and select() (columns) in one sentence?


Speaker Notes: The quickest way to catch a broken pipeline this week is to check the row count after filtering and before computing the final change. Students should be able to say, in one sentence, what each verb did to the data.


Speaker Notes: Before students commit and push, have them answer the last bullet point out loud to a neighbor. If they cannot produce a one-sentence answer distinguishing filter from select, they need to revisit the code. The nrow() check is a quick diagnostic habit that catches silent filter errors — rows that disappear because a condition was mis-specified.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A split-screen diagram showing the same water quality data arranged in wide format on the left (many columns, few rows) and long format on the right (few columns, many rows), with an arrow labeled pivot_longer() pointing from left to right.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce the concept of tidy data and the two primary reshaping functions in tidyr: pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
How To Use Today

Ask whether a variable is hiding in column names.
Count rows before and after every reshape.
Match the data shape to the task: plot, summarize, or present.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Learning Objectives

Explain why wide-format data is difficult to plot in ggplot2.
Use pivot_longer() to reshape wide data into long (tidy) format.
Use pivot_wider() to reshape long data into a wide summary table.
Connect reshaping to downstream plotting and summarization.


Speaker Notes: By the end of today, students will have a concrete mental model: ggplot needs a column of values to map to an aesthetic. Wide format hides values inside column names. pivot_longer() fixes that. Emphasize that this is not an abstract tidyverse concept — it is a practical requirement for making any plot that uses month or parameter as a visual channel.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
The Problem: Wide Data
What is wrong with this?



site_id
nitrate_may
nitrate_jul
nitrate_sep




WQ01
8.4
12.1
9.7


WQ02
7.9
11.3
8.8




Months live in column names, not in a column.
You cannot write aes(x = month) — there is no month column.
Adding a new sampling date means adding new columns, not new rows.


Speaker Notes: Ask students: “If I hand you this table and say ‘make a boxplot of nitrate by month,’ what do you type for x?” Pause. Wait. Let them feel stuck. That discomfort is the exact motivation for pivot_longer(). The problem is not the data values — it is the data shape. ggplot2 maps columns to aesthetics. If months are column names, they cannot be aesthetics.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
The Solution: Long (Tidy) Data
After pivot_longer():



site_id
parameter
month
value




WQ01
nitrate
may
8.4


WQ01
nitrate
jul
12.1


WQ01
nitrate
sep
9.7




Now month is a column — it can be an axis or a fill color.
Each row is one observation.
Adding new dates = new rows, not new columns.


Speaker Notes: This is the tidy data principle from Hadley Wickham’s paper: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell. Wide format violates the “each variable is a column” rule because it stores month as a variable across multiple columns. Walk through the table row by row: WQ01 now has three rows — one for each month. The total rows after pivoting will be 25 sites * 9 measurement columns = 225 rows.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
pivot_longer() Syntax
wq_long <- wq_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = nitrate_may:turbidity_sep,  # which columns to stack
    names_to  = "measurement",              # new column for old names
    values_to = "value"                     # new column for values
  )

cols: the columns being collapsed (use a range or starts_with())
names_to: what to call the column that stores the old column names
values_to: what to call the column that stores the values


Speaker Notes: The argument names trip students up. A memory trick: names_to is where the NAMES go (the old column headers become values in this new column). values_to is where the VALUES go (the actual numbers). Walk through the mapping slowly: “nitrate_may” is a column header in the wide data. After pivoting, it becomes a VALUE in the “measurement” column. The number 8.4 stays a value — it moves into the “value” column.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Row Count Checkpoint
nrow(wq_wide)   # 25 rows
nrow(wq_long)   # 225 rows
Why 225?

25 sites × 9 measurement columns = 225 rows


Speaker Notes: This is the single most important checkpoint of the day. Many students panic when they see 225 rows and think something went wrong. Walk through the math explicitly: we had 25 sites. Each site had 9 measurement columns (nitrate in 3 months + phosphorus in 3 months + turbidity in 3 months = 9). After pivoting, each site contributes 9 rows — one per measurement. 25 × 9 = 225. No data was lost or duplicated. It was just reshaped. Ask: “Is this more or less data than we started with? (Same amount — different shape.)”

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Separating a Combined Column
After pivot_longer(), the measurement column holds values like "nitrate_may".
wq_long <- wq_long |>
  separate(measurement, into = c("parameter", "month"), sep = "_")
Result:



measurement
→
parameter
month




nitrate_may
→
nitrate
may


phosphorus_jul
→
phosphorus
jul


turbidity_sep
→
turbidity
sep




Speaker Notes: The column naming convention in the dataset (parameter_month) was intentional — it makes this separate() step clean. In real-world data, column names are often inconsistent or ambiguous. This is a good moment to discuss naming conventions in data collection: if you collect data yourself, build the separator into your column names from the start so that pivot + separate works automatically. Ask: “Why did I use underscore as the separator and not a space or a period?”

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
pivot_wider() Syntax
wq_summary |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = month,        # column whose values become new column names
    values_from = mean_value    # column whose values fill the table
  )
Useful for: summary tables, not raw analysis.

Speaker Notes: pivot_wider() is the inverse of pivot_longer(). It is most useful when you want to make a readable summary table — for example, showing mean nitrate in each month as side-by-side columns for easy visual comparison. Emphasize that pivot_wider() on raw data often creates problems (like multiple values mapping to one cell), so it is safest to use it after summarizing. The mnemonic: longer = more rows, wider = more columns.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Load water_quality_wide.csv and inspect structure.
Try (and fail) to plot all three months from wide data.
Use pivot_longer() and separate() to create tidy long format.
Build a boxplot: nitrate by month, filled by land use.


Speaker Notes: The “fail first” moment at the start of live coding is intentional pedagogy. Students should try to construct the ggplot from wide data and hit the wall. This creates motivation before the solution is revealed. Do not skip this step — it is the most important teaching moment of the day. After building the working plot from long data, ask: “Which code was harder to write — the failed attempt or this one? Which plot is more informative?”

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Live Coding: Section 2

Use group_by() + summarize() on long data to get mean values.
Use pivot_wider() to turn the summary into a readable table.
Discuss: when is wide format useful?


Speaker Notes: This section connects today’s content back to Week 06 (dplyr). Long format is what dplyr wants for grouped summaries. After summarizing, pivot_wider() can make the result presentable. Reinforce that there is no single “correct” shape for data — the right shape depends on what you are doing with it. Summarizing: long. Plotting: long. Reading a table: sometimes wide. Storing raw data: depends on collection design.

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Watershed Nitrate Audit

Dataset: water_quality_wide.csv
Base goal: Do agricultural watersheds have higher nitrate than forested ones across all three sampling months?
Extension goal: Show the seasonal pattern by month and explain whether the gap changes over time.
Must: pivot to long, group and summarize, then plot.


Speaker Notes: The research question is one that ecologists and regulators actually ask about agricultural watersheds in Nebraska. Nitrate runoff from row crops is a documented water quality concern for the Platte, Elkhorn, and Loup river systems. Students should feel like they are doing real science. The technical requirement — pivot first, then summarize, then plot — mirrors the actual workflow they will use in their own research. Circulate while students work. The most common sticking point is month ordering: students will often get months alphabetically (jul, may, sep) instead of chronologically (may, jul, sep). Ask them: “Does the order on your x-axis tell a true seasonal story?”

title: Week 07: Tidying Data
text:
Verification

Does your long-format data have 225 rows?
Did you use na.rm = TRUE when summarizing?
Are months displayed in seasonal order (May → Jul → Sep)?
Can you state in one sentence why pivot_longer() was necessary?
Can you state in one sentence when pivot_wider() would be useful?


Speaker Notes: Walk through each verification item with the class before they commit. The 225-row check is the most important — it confirms the pivot ran correctly. The na.rm check catches a common mistake that produces NA means silently. The month ordering check is a data communication issue: a plot that shows months alphabetically misrepresents the seasonal trend. The one-sentence explanation forces students to verbalize the core concept, which is the best test of whether they actually understood it.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A diagram showing the data science pipeline as a river flowing from raw field data through cleaning and wrangling to a final visualization, representing the integration of skills learned in Weeks 03-08.
Speaker Notes: These slides frame Week 09 as a capstone synthesis session. No new R syntax is introduced. Students apply everything they have learned in a single integrated workflow on a realistic, messy dataset.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
What We Are Doing Today

No new syntax. Everything you need, you already know.
One realistic messy dataset. One scientific question.
One complete pipeline: import → clean → wrangle → summarize → visualize → interpret.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
How To Use Today

Treat the workflow as one connected pipeline, not separate tricks.
Verify row counts and key values at every step.
If a result looks odd, stop and inspect the data before changing code.


Speaker Notes: This is a milestone session. Weeks 03 through 08 each introduced one piece of the data science puzzle. Today you put all the pieces on the table at once. The data is messier than what you have seen in isolated exercises — deliberately so. Real Nebraska stream data looks like this. The goal is to build confidence that you can navigate a full analysis from start to finish, not just execute individual steps in isolation.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Learning Objectives

Diagnose and describe problems in a raw dataset before writing any cleaning code.
Standardize inconsistent identifiers and categorical values using stringr.
Filter invalid or missing records and track row-count changes at each step.
Summarize EPT richness by site using group_by() and summarize().
Join a site-level lookup table to an analytical summary.
Produce a labeled, publication-ready visualization and interpret the result.


Speaker Notes: Read these objectives out loud with students and ask them to identify which week each skill came from. Objective 2 is Week 05 (strings). Objectives 3 and 4 are Week 06 (dplyr). Objective 5 is Week 07 (joins). Objectives 1 and 6 span everything. This exercise makes students aware of their own accumulated competency.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
The Data Pipeline — A Recap
Raw Data → Import → Inspect → Clean → Wrangle → Summarize → Visualize → Interpret

Each step has a verification check.
Never move to the next step until you can describe what the current step produced.
Row counts are your first diagnostic tool.


Speaker Notes: Draw this pipeline on the whiteboard before opening R. Ask students to tell you what R functions belong in each stage. Import: read_csv(). Inspect: nrow(), str(), head(). Clean: mutate(), str_to_lower(), filter(). Wrangle: group_by(), summarize(). Visualize: ggplot(). The pipeline is not unique to this dataset — it is the template they will use for the rest of their careers.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Today’s Scientific Question

Which Nebraska stream sites show the highest EPT richness, and does richness increase with stream order?


EPT = Ephemeroptera + Plecoptera + Trichoptera
EPT richness is a standard bio-assessment metric: more EPT orders = cleaner water
Dataset: macroinvertebrate field surveys from 10 Nebraska sites, 2022


Speaker Notes: Briefly explain EPT to students who may not have a stream ecology background. Ephemeroptera (mayflies), Plecoptera (stoneflies), and Trichoptera (caddisflies) are pollution-sensitive invertebrate orders. Sites with high EPT richness are generally in better ecological condition. Stream order is a measure of stream size: first-order streams are headwater tributaries; higher-order streams are larger, potentially more disturbed by agriculture and channelization.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
section: The Raw Data: What Could Go Wrong?
text:
The Raw Data: What Could Go Wrong?

SiteID has three formats: "NE01", "ne01", "NE-01"
order_name has three cases: "Ephemeroptera", "ephemeroptera", "EPHEMEROPTERA"
Some count values are NA (not recorded)
Some count values are 0 (recorded absence)
Some dates are YYYY-MM-DD, others are M/D/YYYY


Speaker Notes: Ask students: “Before I write a single line of cleaning code, what would happen if I tried to group_by(SiteID) on the raw data?” They would get 30 groups instead of 10, because ‘NE01’, ‘ne01’, and ‘NE-01’ would each be treated as a distinct site. This is the diagnosis-before-cleaning mindset. Spend 5 minutes on this slide. The skill of noticing problems in data before touching it is underrated and worth emphasizing.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Step 1: Import & Inspect
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(lubridate)

raw <- read_csv(here("data", "macroinvertebrate_raw.csv"))

nrow(raw)
names(raw)
head(raw, 10)
str(raw)
Checkpoint: How many rows? How many unique SiteID values in the raw data?

Speaker Notes: Have students run this code and call out what they see. Expected: 104 rows. If they run count(SiteID) on the raw data they should see 30 groups instead of 10. This is the “aha” moment that motivates the cleaning step. Remind them that str() is their first friend — it tells you the data type of every column, which determines what cleaning functions to use.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Step 2: Standardize Identifiers
cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(
    SiteID     = str_to_upper(SiteID),
    SiteID     = str_remove_all(SiteID, "-"),
    SiteID     = str_trim(SiteID),
    order_name = str_to_lower(str_trim(order_name))
  )

cleaned |> count(SiteID)
cleaned |> count(order_name)
Checkpoint: How many unique SiteID values now? How many unique order_name values?

Speaker Notes: Walk through each mutate line deliberately. str_to_upper() handles case. str_remove_all() with pattern “-” removes the dash. str_trim() removes any stray whitespace. Repeat the same logic for order_name with str_to_lower(). After this step, count(SiteID) should show exactly 10 groups and count(order_name) should show exactly 6 groups. Ask students: ‘What would str_squish() do differently from str_trim()?’ This is a good moment to reinforce that cleaning functions are composable.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Step 3: Filter Invalid Records
filtered <- cleaned |>
  filter(!is.na(count), count > 0)

nrow(filtered)
nrow(cleaned) - nrow(filtered)  # rows removed
Checkpoint: How many rows were removed? What do the removed rows represent?

Speaker Notes: Ask students to decide BEFORE running the code: should we keep zero counts or drop them? There is no universally correct answer. For EPT richness, a count of 0 means the order was not detected — we drop it because we want presence only. For abundance models, zeros are meaningful and must be retained. The point is that this is a scientific decision, not a coding decision. The code just implements the decision.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Step 5: Join to Site Lookup
site_lookup <- tibble(
  SiteID    = c("NE01", "NE02", "NE03", "NE04", "NE05",
                "NE06", "NE07", "NE08", "NE09", "NE10"),
  watershed = c("Platte", "Platte", "Loup", "Loup", "Elkhorn",
                "Elkhorn", "Platte", "Loup", "Elkhorn", "Platte")
)

ept_joined <- ept_summary |>
  left_join(site_lookup, by = "SiteID")

ept_joined |> filter(is.na(watershed))
Checkpoint: Did every site get a watershed? Why use left_join and not inner_join?

Speaker Notes: The inline tibble is intentional — no extra file to track, no path issues. Ask students why left_join was chosen. A left_join keeps all rows from the left table (ept_summary) and adds matching columns from the right (site_lookup). If any SiteID in ept_summary was missing from site_lookup, that row would have NA in the watershed column — and the filter() check at the end would expose it. inner_join would silently drop unmatched sites, which is usually more dangerous.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Step 6: Visualize
ggplot(ept_joined, aes(x = factor(stream_order), y = ept_richness)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = watershed), size = 4, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title    = "EPT Richness by Stream Order",
    subtitle = "Nebraska macroinvertebrate sites, 2022",
    x        = "Stream Order",
    y        = "EPT Richness (# of EPT orders present)",
    color    = "Watershed"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Speaker Notes: Before they run the code, ask: “Should stream_order be numeric or a factor on the x-axis?” As numeric, ggplot would draw a continuous axis and might try to fit a smooth line — misleading because stream order is an ordinal categorical variable, not truly continuous. factor() forces a discrete axis. Also point out scale_color_brewer() — this is from Week 04. Color-blind safe palettes should be the default, not the exception.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Interpretation

Does EPT richness increase with stream order?
Which watershed has the most consistently high EPT richness?
What caveats would you include in a figure caption?


Speaker Notes: Push students to interpret, not just describe. ‘The plot shows points’ is description. ‘Sites with higher stream order tend to have higher EPT richness, suggesting larger streams in this dataset support more pollution-sensitive taxa — though sample size per stream order is small’ is interpretation with appropriate epistemic humility. Remind them that any claim should be proportional to the sample size and design of the data.

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
The Weekly Challenge [45 mins]
Your Task
Using macroinvertebrate_raw.csv:

Import and diagnose the data (5 min)
Standardize SiteID and order_name (10 min)
Filter zeros and NAs (5 min)
Summarize EPT richness by site (10 min)
Join to the site lookup (5 min)
Plot and interpret (10 min)

Base goal: Produce a correct site-level EPT summary and plot.
Extension goal: Compare richness and abundance as separate stories.
Verification: Check row counts at every step. Do not skip.

Speaker Notes: Give students the time budget out loud and post it on the screen. Walk the room during Steps 2 and 4 — those are where most students will need support. Students who finish early should try the extension: replace ept_richness with ept_abundance as the y-axis and compare the two plots. Do they tell the same story?

title: Week 09: Integrated Challenge I
text:
Verification Before You Commit

Raw data: 104 rows, 7 columns
After standardization: still 104 rows, 10 unique SiteIDs, 6 unique order_names
After filtering: fewer rows (check: how many removed?)
EPT summary: 10 rows, one per site
Join: 0 NAs in watershed column
Plot renders with labeled axes and a professional theme
You can explain why each step belongs in the order shown


Speaker Notes: Read through this checklist with students before they close their laptops. This verification pattern — state your expectations first, then check — is what separates professional-grade analysis from student-grade analysis. If any check fails, that is not a problem; it is information. The goal is to never let a mistake pass silently.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A time-series line chart showing stream discharge measurements across multiple river monitoring sites over the course of a calendar year, with peaks visible in spring months.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce lubridate for parsing mixed-format date strings and ggplot2 for visualizing time-series data from environmental sensors.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
Week 11: Dates and Time Series
section: Why Dates Are Harder Than They Look
text:
Why Dates Are Harder Than They Look

Date strings look simple — they are not.
R reads date_recorded as character when formats are mixed.
Silent failures: as.Date("May 15, 2023") returns NA with no error.
Today: tools that handle the mess.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
How To Use Today

Parse first, then summarize or plot.
Check for NA immediately after parsing.
Use ordered date components when the chart needs calendar meaning.


Speaker Notes: Open with this question: “Has anyone ever loaded a date column and gotten NAs they didn’t expect?” Almost every student will raise their hand. That’s the point — the default tools fail silently on mixed formats. lubridate’s parse_date_time() is the fix, and today we’ll understand why.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Learning Objectives

Recognize and name common date string formats (ISO 8601, US slash, spelled month).
Use parse_date_time() to handle mixed-format date columns.
Extract components: year(), month(), yday().
Aggregate time series with floor_date().
Build and interpret time-series line plots in ggplot2.


Speaker Notes: These five objectives form a complete workflow — you cannot plot a time series correctly until you have parsed the dates correctly, and you cannot aggregate sensibly without floor_date. Emphasize that parsing is the foundation; everything else sits on top of it.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Common Date Formats



Format Name
Example
lubridate order




ISO 8601
2023-05-15
"ymd"


US slash
05/15/2023
"mdy"


Spelled month
May 15, 2023
"BdY"


Spelled compact
May 15 2023
"BdY"


European
15/05/2023
"dmy"



Mixed formats in one column are the norm in sensor data, not the exception.

Speaker Notes: Walk through each row in the table. Point out the ISO 8601 standard specifically — it is unambiguous (year always first, largest unit to smallest) and is the preferred format for any data you create. US slash format is the most dangerous because “05/06/2023” could be May 6 or June 5 depending on locale. Spelled month is verbose but unambiguous.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
parse_date_time() vs as.Date()
# as.Date() fails silently on unrecognized formats
as.Date("May 15, 2023")   # returns NA — no warning by default

# parse_date_time() tries multiple formats in order
parse_date_time(
  "May 15, 2023",
  orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "BdY")
)
# [1] "2023-05-15 UTC"
Always check: sum(is.na(date_parsed)) after parsing.

Speaker Notes: Live-type the as.Date() example first and show the NA. Then show parse_date_time(). Pause and ask: “What would happen to your analysis if 15 out of 120 rows silently became NA and you didn’t check?” That’s a missing-data problem that masquerades as a date problem. The check — sum(is.na()) — is the safety net.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Extracting Date Components
library(lubridate)

discharge <- discharge |>
  mutate(
    yr     = year(date_parsed),
    mo     = month(date_parsed, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    mo_num = month(date_parsed),
    doy    = yday(date_parsed)
  )

month(label = TRUE) returns an ordered factor — plots sort correctly.
yday() is useful for phenology and day-of-year comparisons across years.


Speaker Notes: Ask students: “Why do we want month as an ordered factor instead of a character string?” The answer is that ggplot2 will sort character strings alphabetically — so April comes before August comes before February. An ordered factor with levels Jan-Dec plots in calendar order automatically. This is a common bug students hit when they forget label = TRUE.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
floor_date: Snapping to Periods
floor_date(as.Date("2023-05-15"), unit = "month")
# [1] "2023-05-01"

floor_date(as.Date("2023-05-15"), unit = "week")
# [1] "2023-05-14"  (snaps to Sunday by default)
Use floor_date() as the x-axis grouping key for aggregated time series.
discharge |>
  mutate(month_floor = floor_date(date_parsed, unit = "month")) |>
  group_by(site_id, month_floor) |>
  summarise(mean_q = mean(discharge_cfs, na.rm = TRUE))

Speaker Notes: The key mental model: floor_date does for dates what floor() does for numbers — it rounds down to the nearest period boundary. Show on the board: if you have readings on May 3, May 17, and May 29, floor_date maps all three to May 1. Now you can group by that “May 1” key and get a true monthly average. Without this, group_by(date) would give you one row per date, not per month.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Plotting Time Series with ggplot2
ggplot(monthly_discharge,
       aes(x = month_floor, y = mean_discharge, color = site_id)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_datetime(
    date_breaks  = "2 months",
    date_labels  = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Mean Discharge — Platte River Sites",
       x = "Month", y = "Mean Discharge (cfs)") +
  theme_minimal()

Speaker Notes: Point out scale_x_datetime() specifically — this is the scale for POSIXct columns (what parse_date_time returns). If the column were a Date (not POSIXct), you would use scale_x_date() instead. The date_labels argument uses strftime format codes: %b = abbreviated month name, %Y = 4-digit year. A gap in a geom_line means missing data — lines do not connect across NAs. Ask students to look for gaps as a data-quality check.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Load stream_discharge.csv and inspect the date column.
Identify the three date formats across sites.
Parse with parse_date_time() and verify no NAs.
Extract year(), month(), yday().
Create month_floor with floor_date().


Speaker Notes: Before opening RStudio, have students predict: how many rows will have date parse failures? Take a show of hands for different guesses. Then run the code and check together. The goal is to build the habit of verifying before moving on — not assuming the parse worked.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Live Coding: Section 2

Aggregate to monthly mean discharge by site.
Plot the time series — identify the seasonal peak.
Compute a seasonal summary across all sites.
Discuss: which site shows the most flow variability?


Speaker Notes: When the plot renders, give students 60 seconds to silently look at it before asking questions. Then ask: “Which month appears to be peak discharge?” and “Are all six sites synchronized, or do some peak earlier?” These questions prepare them for the challenge.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Platte River Pulse

“Does discharge peak in spring across all monitoring sites, and which site has the most variable flow?”

Steps Required: 1. Parse all dates (use the script from the demo). 2. Extract month and calculate monthly mean and SD by site. 3. Calculate coefficient of variation (CV = SD / mean) per site. 4. Identify the highest-CV site. 5. Plot seasonal pattern by site — colored or faceted.
Base goal: Build the monthly summary and identify the peak discharge month.
Extension goal: Compare variability across sites with CV and explain the pattern.

Speaker Notes: The coefficient of variation is new to some students — define it: it is the standard deviation expressed as a proportion of the mean. A high CV means the flow varies a lot relative to its average level. Sites near reservoirs or regulated reaches tend to have lower CV; unregulated streams have higher CV. Students should interpret their result in that ecological context.

title: Week 11: Dates and Time Series
text:
Verification

Does sum(is.na(date_parsed)) equal 0?
Does the line plot x-axis show month names in calendar order?
Can you identify the peak discharge month from the plot?
Which site has the highest coefficient of variation?
Did you use na.rm = TRUE in all summary calculations?
Can you explain why floor_date() is the grouping key for monthly summaries?


Speaker Notes: Walk through each bullet as a class. For the third bullet, ask a student to name the peak month without looking at the data summary — they should be able to read it from the plot. If they cannot, the plot labels need work. For the last bullet, remind students that discharge_cfs has 5 NAs — forgetting na.rm = TRUE will propagate those NAs into every group containing a missing value.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A diagram showing a single labeled box labeled “function” receiving two arrows on the left (inputs) and producing one arrow on the right (output), representing the abstraction of repeated logic.
Speaker Notes: These slides introduce writing R functions as a tool for eliminating repeated pipeline code, with a direct connection to capstone project reproducibility.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Where We Are

We have now filtered, summarized, visualized, and iterated over data.
We have used purrr::map() to apply operations across lists.
Today: We wrap those operations into named, testable, reusable functions.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
How To Use Today

Write the function once, then test it on more than one input.
Keep the body readable by reusing the pipelines you already know.
Add a check that fails early if the inputs are wrong.


Speaker Notes: Take 2 minutes to orient the class. We are at Week 13 of 15. Everything we have built this semester has been a setup for this moment. Functions are the glue that holds a reproducible analysis together. If a student can write one clean function today, they are ready to clean up their capstone pipeline.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Learning Objectives

Write a function with function(), arguments, a body, and return().
Apply the DRY principle to eliminate copy-pasted pipeline code.
Validate function inputs with stopifnot().
Use a function inside map() and mutate().


Speaker Notes: Read these aloud and ask students to keep them in mind. By the end of today, they should be able to do all four. The assignment will ask them to demonstrate 1 through 4 using their own capstone data. That connection — today’s skill, their real data — is the through-line for the session.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
The DRY Principle
Don’t Repeat Yourself
# Copy-pasted code: 3 places to break
fw |> filter(state == "NE") |> group_by(species_code) |> summarize(...)
fw |> filter(state == "IA") |> group_by(species_code) |> summarize(...)
fw |> filter(state == "KS") |> group_by(species_code) |> summarize(...)

# DRY: one place to maintain
summarize_species(fw, "NE")
summarize_species(fw, "IA")
summarize_species(fw, "KS")

Speaker Notes: Ask the class: “If I need to change the filter from January to February, how many lines do I edit in the top version? In the bottom version?” The answer — three versus one — is the entire argument for functions in one question. Copy-paste is not a strategy; it is deferred debt. Every duplicated block is a bug waiting to happen during the capstone crunch week.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Default Arguments
# n_top = 5 is the default — caller does not have to pass it
summarize_species(fw, "NE")        # returns top 5
summarize_species(fw, "NE", n_top = 3)  # overrides default

Default arguments make a function flexible and easy to call.
Put defaults on arguments that have a sensible “most common” value.
Arguments without defaults must be supplied by the caller.


Speaker Notes: Live-code both calls so students see the output change when n_top is overridden. Then ask: “What happens if I don’t pass data?” They should predict an error. Run it to confirm. The lesson: arguments without defaults are required; arguments with defaults are optional. This is a design decision — think about what the caller will need most of the time.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Validate Inputs with stopifnot()
summarize_species <- function(data, state_filter, n_top = 5) {

  stopifnot(
    "data must be a data frame" = is.data.frame(data),
    "state_filter must be a single string" =
      is.character(state_filter) && length(state_filter) == 1
  )

  # ... rest of body
}

A bad input should fail loudly and immediately, not silently downstream.
The named form "message" = condition gives the caller a helpful error.


Speaker Notes: Run the function with a bad argument — e.g., pass 42 as state_filter — and show the error message. Then ask: “Without stopifnot(), what would the filter() call return? Would it be an error or an empty tibble?” It would likely be a silent empty tibble — which is far harder to debug. The principle: fail early with a clear message, not late with a confusing result. This is especially important for capstone code that others (or future-you) will run.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Functions + map()
# Week 12 recap: map() applies a function to each element
states <- c("NE", "IA", "KS")

# Apply our function to each state
result_list <- map(states, \(s) summarize_species(fw, s))

# Bind list of tibbles into one data frame
all_results <- list_rbind(result_list)

map() replaces a for-loop with a cleaner, functional pattern.
list_rbind() stacks the list of tibbles into a single data frame.


Speaker Notes: This is the payoff slide — the function we wrote drops directly into the map() pattern from Week 12. Ask: “How many lines of code would this have been if we had copied the pipeline three times?” Then contrast with 3 lines using map(). Run this live so students see the list_rbind() output. Point out that adding a fourth state requires changing only the states vector — nothing else in the pipeline changes.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The State Species Auditor
Write a top_n_species() function that:

Takes data, state_filter, and n (default 5).
Returns a ranked species summary with total_obs, n_sites, and rank.
Includes at least one input validation (stopifnot or if/stop).

Then: - Test it on NE and IA individually. - Apply it via map() to a list of at least 3 states. - Bind results and make a faceted bar plot.
Base goal: Get the function working for one state with one clear output.
Extension goal: Generalize it cleanly enough to map across multiple states.

Speaker Notes: Read the three requirements aloud before students start. Emphasize constraint 3 — the validation — because it is easy to skip under time pressure and it is the hardest habit to build. Walk the room during the 45 minutes. When students finish the base goal, push them toward the extension: add a month_filter argument that defaults to NULL (all months) but can be set to a single month number.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Verification

Does your function return the right number of rows when n = 5? n = 3?
Does it fail with a clear error when you pass 42 as state_filter?
Does map() return a list of the correct length?
Can you explain what return() does without using the word “return”?
Can you point to the one line that makes the function reusable?


Speaker Notes: Work through these questions as a class. The last question — explain return() without using the word return — is a good comprehension check. A strong answer: “It hands a value back to whoever called the function so they can store it or use it.” Before closing, connect to the assignment: students will write a function for their OWN capstone data. Ask 2-3 students to name one pipeline step in their project that they have repeated. Those are tomorrow’s functions.

title: Week 13: Functions for Repeated Work
text:
Capstone Connection

“Every pipeline step you have copy-pasted more than once is a function waiting to be written.”


Assignment 13: Write one cleaning or summarization function for your capstone dataset.
Test it on two different inputs.
Render a Quarto report showing the function and its outputs.
Due: Sunday, Nov 22, 11:59 PM


Speaker Notes: End on this framing. Students are 2 weeks from capstone submissions. The assignment is not busywork — it is the first step of their final cleanup. Encourage them to use a real piece of their capstone pipeline, not a toy example. The function they write this week may end up in their final report.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A GitHub Pull Request interface showing review comments anchored to specific lines of code, representing the professional peer review workflow.
Speaker Notes: These slides guide students through the GitHub Pull Request review workflow, covering how to write actionable review comments, open methodological Issues, and respond to feedback with traceable commits.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Where We Are

Week 15 of 16 — your capstone drafts are in.
Today: you review a classmate’s draft; a classmate reviews yours.
Skill being practiced: professional code review — a core workflow in data science, government agencies, and academic research teams.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
How To Use Today

Review the draft as if you were trying to reproduce it from scratch.
Make comments specific enough that the author can act on them immediately.
Separate required fixes from open discussion.


Speaker Notes: Remind students that code review is not grading each other. The goal is to help the author make the project more reproducible, clearer, and analytically sound. Frame it as a collaboration, not a critique. Many students have never seen a professional pull request workflow; today normalizes it.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Learning Objectives

Write a PR description that makes a reviewer’s job tractable.
Post review comments that are specific, located, and actionable.
Distinguish between a PR comment (must fix) and a GitHub Issue (must discuss).
Respond to received feedback with a commit that explains what changed and why.


Speaker Notes: These four objectives map directly to the assignment rubric. Walk through each one briefly before diving into the demo. Emphasize that objective 3 — the PR vs Issue distinction — is the subtlest and the one students most often get wrong.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Why Code Review Exists

In industry: No code ships without a second pair of eyes.
In science: Reproducibility requires that someone else can run your code.
For you: The review process catches errors that familiarity blinds you to.


“Code is read far more often than it is written.” — Guido van Rossum


Speaker Notes: Students sometimes feel that review is adversarial. Share the van Rossum quote and follow up: “Your code will be read by future-you, by your advisor, by collaborators, and now by a classmate. Writing for a reader is a professional skill.” Ask if anyone has returned to their own code after six months and not understood it.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
The Pull Request Workflow

Author pushes a branch and opens a PR with a clear description.
Reviewer reads the description, clones/renders, and posts line-level comments.
Author responds to each comment with a commit (or a reply explaining why not).
Reviewer confirms changes and approves or requests another round.
Author (or instructor) merges.


Speaker Notes: Draw this as a loop on the whiteboard: Author → PR → Reviewer → Comments → Author (commits) → Reviewer (approves) → Merge. Stress that step 3 is where most students stall. Responding to every comment — even to say “I disagree, and here is why” — is required professional behavior. Silence is not a valid response to a review comment.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
section: Anatomy of a Good PR Description
text:
Anatomy of a Good PR Description
A PR description must answer three questions:

What changed? — What will the reviewer see in the diff?
Why? — The scientific or analytical reason for the change.
How do I verify it? — Step-by-step reproduction instructions.


Speaker Notes: Show the bad example first on GitHub: “Fixed some stuff. Should work now.” Ask the class: “If you were reviewing this, where would you even start?” Then show the good template. The key insight is that a PR description is written for the reviewer, not for the author. The author already knows what changed.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Good PR Description vs Bad


Bad

Fixed some stuff. Should work now.


Good

What changed: Replaced setwd() on line 14 with here::here().
Why: The old path only ran on my machine.
Verify: Clone fresh → open .Rproj → knit → confirm all figures appear.



Speaker Notes: Ask the class to identify why the bad version fails before revealing the good version. Common student answers: “we don’t know what ‘stuff’ means,” “we can’t verify anything.” Push further: “What does ‘should work now’ tell the reviewer about scientific validity?” Answer: nothing.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
section: Writing a Review Comment: The Formula
text:
Writing a Review Comment: The Formula
Every substantive comment should contain:

Location — file name and line number (GitHub anchors this automatically)
Observation — what you actually see in the code or output
Concern — why it matters (reproducibility, inference, clarity)
Suggestion — a concrete alternative, ideally as a code snippet


Speaker Notes: Walk through this formula on the demo repo. Show students how to click a line number in GitHub’s “Files Changed” tab to open a comment box anchored to that line. Emphasize that “Suggestion” is where students often write vague advice instead of a concrete fix. If you can write the replacement code in four lines, write it.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Good Comment vs Bad Comment


Bad

This looks wrong.


I think you should reorganize this.


Why did you do it this way?


Good

Line 47 — hard-coded path read_csv('/Users/student/Desktop/...') will not run on another machine. Replace with here('data', 'fish.csv'). This is required for reproducibility.



Speaker Notes: Show the bad comments on screen and ask: “What would you do with this feedback as an author?” The answer is usually “not much — I don’t know what to fix.” Then show the good comment and ask: “How long would it take to act on this?” Usually under two minutes. That specificity is the point. Also note that “Why did you do it this way?” is not inherently bad — it belongs in a GitHub Issue, not a PR comment, because it opens a discussion rather than identifying a required fix.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
PR Comment vs GitHub Issue









PR Comment
GitHub Issue




Use when
Something must change
Something must be discussed


Tone
“Please fix X”
“I have a question about decision Y”


Resolves when
Author pushes a fix
Parties agree on an approach


Example
Hard-coded path
Whether to exclude outlier year




Speaker Notes: The hardest part of this distinction is that methodological questions often FEEL like they should be PR comments. Walk through the outlier example: if you write “Remove the 2019 data” as a PR comment, you are making the decision for the author. Opening an Issue says “I noticed this — let’s discuss.” The author may have a good reason for including 2019. Issues preserve the conversation and the decision rationale, which is good for the scientific record.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
The Reproducibility Checklist
Before posting any review comment, verify:

Can you clone and render without editing anything?
Are all file paths project-relative (no setwd(), no absolute paths)?
Are missing data decisions documented (how many rows, which column, why)?
Does every figure have a caption describing the trend?
Are conclusions supported by visible output in the rendered document?
Is the README clear enough for a new reader to start?


Speaker Notes: Walk through the checklist item by item. For item 1, remind students that “renders on my machine” is not the same as “reproducible.” They need to actually clone to a new directory and try. For item 3, emphasize that na.omit() is the silent killer — it removes rows without telling the reader how many or from where. For item 5, tell students to cover the prose and look only at the figures and tables — can they reconstruct the conclusions?

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
section: Responding to Review: The Author’s Role
text:
Responding to Review: The Author’s Role
When you receive comments on your PR:

Read all comments before responding — some may be related.
For each comment: push a fix OR reply explaining why you disagree.
Commit messages matter: say WHAT changed and WHY, reference the comment.
After pushing: resolve the conversation and @mention the reviewer.


Speaker Notes: Students often address comments one at a time and push after each fix, which creates a noisy commit history. Recommend batching related fixes into one commit. The commit message is a permanent record of the decision. Show on the demo repo: “fix: replace hard-coded path with here() — addresses review comment #3 in PR #7” vs “addressed comments.” Future-you will thank you for the first version.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Good Commit Message vs Bad


Bad

addressed comments


fixed it


update


Good

fix: replace hard-coded path with here() on line 47
Reviewer flagged that the absolute path broke on other machines. Also updated README to note the here() convention. Resolves review comment #3 in PR #7.



Speaker Notes: Run git log --oneline on the demo repo and show what a history of “addressed comments / fixed it / update” looks like — three identical-looking commits with no information. Then show a clean history. Ask students: “If your advisor asked you in six months what you changed between draft 1 and draft 2, which history would help you answer?” The good history is also evidence of responsiveness, which matters for the assignment rubric.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Peer Review Rubric








Criterion
Points
What earns full marks




Reproducibility check
3
All checklist items evaluated; clone-and-render tested


Comment quality
4
3+ comments with location, observation, concern, and suggestion


GitHub Issue
2
1+ issue with context, question, and proposed next steps


Revision commits
3
2+ commits responding to received feedback with clear messages


Total
12





Speaker Notes: Walk through each row. Stress that “comment quality” is not about harshness — a polite, specific comment that gives the author a clear path forward earns full marks. A harsh but vague comment earns nothing. For “revision commits,” remind students that the commit message is the evidence — the grader will read it.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Today’s Workflow

0:00 – 0:30 — GitHub PR demo (live, follow along)
0:30 – 0:45 — Issues demo + Q&A
0:45 – 1:00 — Work time: clone partner’s repo and run the reproducibility checklist
1:00 – 1:15 — Break
1:15 – 2:15 — Write and post review comments + open Issue
2:15 – 2:45 — Respond to received feedback with revision commits
2:45 – 3:00 — Wrap-up and submission instructions


Speaker Notes: Keep the demo tight — 30 minutes is enough if you have a prepared demo repo with a realistic but intentionally flawed analysis script. The most valuable class time is the second half when students are writing and responding to real reviews. Be available to walk around during the work periods. Common sticking points: students not knowing how to anchor a comment to a line in GitHub, and students not understanding that they need to push AFTER making edits.

title: Week 15: Code Review and Revision
text:
Verification

Did you clone your partner’s repo and confirm it renders?
Did you post 3+ substantive comments (location + observation + concern + suggestion)?
Did you open at least 1 GitHub Issue for a methodological question?
Did you push 2+ revision commits responding to feedback on YOUR repo?
Do your commit messages explain what changed and why?
Can you explain why a methodological disagreement belongs in an Issue rather than a PR comment?


Speaker Notes: Read through the verification list before releasing students for the work period. This is the same list on the assignment rubric. Tell students: “If you can answer yes to all five of these by the end of class, you are on track. The written submission is due Sunday — use the remaining time to finish anything incomplete.”
